quote: It would violate Conservation of Energy. And the Second Law of Thermodynamics. And just about every other law of physics.
content: The first of these is the one the essay names first and it is the wrong reason. In an expanding universe the photon’s energy is not conserved: it redshifts, and there is no global energy conservation law in general relativity for the photon’s vanishing to violate (the annotation on Universal Law gives the references). A photon that redshifts without limit does approach, in every measurable respect, the state of not being there, and the difference between “it is still there with vanishing energy” and “it is gone” is not a difference any conservation law adjudicates. The essay’s conclusion is nonetheless right, for the reason the essay gives later: the disappearance would require an additional law, keyed to the observer’s horizon, and no such law is in the theory. That is a parsimony argument, and it would have been better to give it alone than to lead with a conservation law that the cosmology in question suspends.

quote: Though I failed to Google a source, I remember reading that when it was first proposed that the Milky Way was our galaxy—that the hazy river of light in the night sky was made up of millions (or even billions) of stars—that Occam’s Razor was invoked against the new hypothesis.
content: No such episode is recorded, and the essay says as much. Galileo resolved the Milky Way into stars with his telescope in 1610 and reported it in Sidereus Nuncius without recorded objection on grounds of parsimony; the argument in the “island universe” debate from Kant (1755) and Wright through the Curtis–Shapley Great Debate of 1920 was about distances, novae and the rotation measurements of van Maanen, not about the number of entities. The essay needs a historical case in which Occam’s razor was misapplied against a large universe, and, unable to find one, uses a memory of one. That is a small thing in itself; it is the same pattern the annotations on Book I found in the history of science there, and a paragraph built on a source the author could not locate is exactly what The Beauty of Settled Science, six essays earlier, warned the reader against trusting in the press.

quote: It’s not that you believe in the invisible as such, from reasoning about invisible things. Rather the experimental evidence supports certain laws, and belief in those laws logically implies the existence of certain entities that you can’t interact with. This is belief in the implied invisible.
content: The argument is that Solomonoff induction and Minimum Message Length, which do not penalize a model for describing more stuff, license belief in the stuff. They do not, and the gap is the oldest dispute in philosophy of science. Solomonoff’s prior is over programs that generate the observer’s data stream; the shortest such program encodes the laws, and the photon beyond the horizon is not in the data stream and never will be, so the formalism assigns it nothing at all. Believing in it is an interpretive step, scientific realism, taken on top of the formalism, and the constructive empiricist takes the other step: accept the laws as empirically adequate, remain agnostic about what they say of the unobservable (van Fraassen, The Scientific Image, 1980). Van Fraassen can run Solomonoff induction as happily as the essay can; what he declines is the inference from “the simplest description of my observations posits X” to “X exists,” and the essay’s principle of the implied invisible is that inference, with the word “logically” doing the work of an argument that is not given. There are good arguments for realism (the no-miracles argument, structural realism); “the equations imply it” is not one of them, since the equations are the description whose reference is in question. The colony ship at the end is a nice case, and it is decided by which of these positions one holds, not by Occam.
